documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT
32 y/o F transferring her care from her prior primary care office. Wanted a doctor she can message between visits.

CC: corners of the mouth cracking, tongue sore, rash next to her nose and in her eyebrows. About four weeks.

HPI: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass March 2024, roughly 150 lb down since. Ever since surgery she has had nausea most days and throws up every so often; on the bad days she barely eats. The splits at the corners of her mouth sting with anything salty or acidic, and her tongue feels raw. Red, flaky patches beside the nose and through the brows, only mildly itchy. Vaseline on the lips hasn't helped. No fever, no mouth ulcers, no diarrhea. Says she takes her supplements most days, misses some when nauseated.

PMH: severe preeclampsia with her prior pregnancy, delivered at 34 wk. Morbid obesity before the bypass, resolved. Malabsorption after bypass.
PSH: RYGB 3/2024. Preterm delivery at 34 wk.
Meds: prenatal vitamin daily; vitamin B complex daily; ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily; calcium citrate + vit D 600 mg/400 IU twice a day.
Allergies: NKDA.
FH: mother - severe preeclampsia. Maternal grandmother - chronic HTN. Father - type 2 DM.
SH: elementary school teacher. Never smoked. No alcohol. No drugs.

Exam: vitals as charted. Comfortable, conversant.
Mouth: fissured, red skin at both oral commissures. Tongue red, smooth, a little swollen.
Skin: erythematous patches with greasy scale in both nasolabial folds and the eyebrows.
Neck supple, no adenopathy. Heart RRR. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender, small healed laparoscopic scars. Ext without edema.
PHQ-2 0.

A/P
1. Angular cheilitis, glossitis and a seborrheic-looking facial rash in a bypass patient with poor intake. Suspect a vitamin deficiency. Referral to GI for bypass/nutrition evaluation and labs; keep taking all supplements daily.
2. s/p RYGB with malabsorption, ongoing nausea and occasional vomiting. Small meals, sip fluids through the day.
3. Hx severe preeclampsia - flagged for any future pregnancy.
4. Hx morbid obesity, resolved after bypass.

Records release signed for prior PCP and the bariatric program. Will see her back after GI.

documents.title: Gastroenterology Consultation
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
GASTROENTEROLOGY CONSULTATION
Date of service: 09/29/2025
Requested by: primary care
Question: mouth, tongue and facial skin changes after gastric bypass

Ms. Cronin is a 32-year-old woman seen at your request. Over the last two months she has developed painful splitting at the angles of the mouth, a sore tongue, and a persistent rash around the nose and eyebrows. Her Roux-en-Y gastric bypass was about 18 months ago and she has lost close to 150 pounds. Nausea has persisted since surgery with occasional emesis, and by her account her diet has been poor as a result.

Past history: severe preeclampsia in a previous pregnancy requiring delivery at 34 weeks; RYGB complicated by malabsorption; morbid obesity before surgery, now resolved.
Medications: prenatal vitamin daily; vitamin B complex daily; ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily; calcium citrate/vitamin D 600 mg/400 IU twice daily.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.
Family history: mother with severe preeclampsia; maternal grandmother with chronic hypertension; father with type 2 diabetes.
Social: teaches elementary school. Never smoker, abstains from alcohol.

Examination: vitals per clinic intake. Bilateral angular cheilitis. The tongue is beefy red and swollen. Greasy, scaling erythematous eruption confined to the nasolabial folds and eyebrows. Abdomen soft and nontender with well-healed laparoscopic port sites.

Laboratory (09/29/2025):
Hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, MCV 84 fL, MCHC 32 g/dL
Iron 80 mcg/dL, TIBC 300 mcg/dL
Vitamin B12 400 pg/mL
Folate 10 ng/mL
Plasma riboflavin (resulted 10/06/2025) 2.4 nmol/L, reference 6.2-39.0, LOW

Impression: Riboflavin (vitamin B2) deficiency following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, from malabsorption compounded by poor oral intake. The cheilitis, glossitis and seborrheic-pattern dermatitis together are typical. Red cell indices are normocytic and iron, B12 and folate are within range.

Recommendations:
1. Riboflavin 100 mg by mouth once daily for approximately three months.
2. Continue the prenatal vitamin, B complex, iron and calcium citrate with D.
3. Small, protein-first meals spread through the day.
4. Recheck plasma riboflavin at the end of the course; this can be drawn with her primary care labs.

We are happy to see her again if needed.

documents.title: Obstetrics New Prenatal Visit
documents.author: obstetrics
documents.body:
OBSTETRICS - NEW PRENATAL VISIT
Visit date: 06/29/2026
Referred by: primary care

Ms. Cronin is a 33-year-old seen for her first prenatal visit, 10 weeks 0 days by LMP 04/20/2026, EDD 01/25/2027.

She comes to us with a prior pregnancy complicated by severe preeclampsia that required delivery at 34 weeks. She also had a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass in 2024 and was treated last fall for riboflavin deficiency, which has since resolved. This pregnancy has gone smoothly so far. She is taking her prenatal vitamin daily and describes a balanced diet. Her main question today was what else she can do to lower her chance of preeclampsia this time.

Medications: prenatal vitamin daily; vitamin B complex daily; ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily; calcium citrate/vitamin D 600 mg/400 IU twice daily.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.
Family history: mother - severe preeclampsia; maternal grandmother - chronic hypertension; father - type 2 diabetes.
Social: elementary school teacher; never smoker; no alcohol.

Vitals: BP 128/82 mmHg. BMI 35 kg/m2.

Assessment: Pregnancy at 10 weeks, high risk on the basis of prior severe preeclampsia with preterm delivery and prior bariatric surgery.

Plan:
- Low-dose aspirin 81 mg by mouth daily, beginning at 12 weeks and continuing through the pregnancy, to reduce the risk of recurrent preeclampsia. Reviewed the rationale with her.
- Continue prenatal vitamin and her bariatric supplements unchanged.
- Return visit in 4 weeks.

Thank you for involving us in her care; we will keep you informed.
